body: We should be able to figure out what modules are included from the defaults + command-line options, and use those to populate `env["VSHINT_INCLUDES"]`, if that turns out to be the proper solution, right?

One approach that seems to work as you describe is to append to `VSHINT_DEFINES` or `VSHINT_INCLUDES` right after the appropriate `SCsub` file appends to their local environment. Two examples of this:

In `modules/SCsub`:
```python
# Allow modules to detect if they are being built as a module.
env_modules.Append(CPPDEFINES=["GODOT_MODULE"])
env.Append(VSHINT_DEFINES=["GODOT_MODULE"]) # adding this line defines GODOT_MODULE in the generated vsproj
```

In `modules/text_server_adv/SCsub`:
```python
env_harfbuzz.Prepend(CPPPATH=["#thirdparty/harfbuzz/src"])
env.Append(VSHINT_INCLUDES=["thirdparty/harfbuzz/src"]) #adding this line adds the include search path in generated vsproj
```

Of course, requiring this to be done manually in every instance is error-prone and tedious. A way around that might be to define a helper function in `methods.py` for these actions? Something like:
```python
# A more robust version could take in a list of paths instead of just one path.
def add_cpp_include_path(env, path):
    env.Prepend(CPPPATH=[path])
    # If there's no way to get the root env from a child env, maybe the root env would need to be passed in?
    # Also, the '#' sign doesn't seem to work in VSHINT_INCLUDES, so it would need to be stripped here.
    env.root.Append(VSHINT_INCLUDES=[path])

def add_cpp_define(env, path):
    # Same idea here...
```

And then the function can be called on an env later on instead of manually appending to `CPPPATH` or `CPPDEFINES`:
```python
env.add_cpp_include_path("#thirdparty/harfbuzz/src")
```

FYI, that is precisely why `VSHINT_INCLUDES` and `VSHINT_DEFINES` exist, yes, I just didn't get around to putting them in every codepath. I agree that manually adding them is brittle, and also, these are global-level defines, and not all defines are meant to be global, some are meant to apply only to the particular set of code being built (and might actually contradict global defines). So adding them to the VS project requires a bit of care. With that said, the examples you give here are probably safe to add to VS as global settings (also see #112154 for more fixes around this)
